newsitem.title: JORDAN: Jordan to replace food rations with cash handouts.
newsitem.headline: Jordan to replace food rations with cash handouts.

text.p: Jordan plans by September to replace food rationing with cash handouts for most citizens, the last major hurdle to liberalising a costly subsidy programme, officials said on Sunday.
The move will eliminate a ration card system which offers substantial allotments of rice, sugar and powdered milk at subsidised prices to over 90 percent of Jordanians every three months.

The cash handouts are similar to a scheme introduced last year to cut bread subsidies, a move that sparked rioting in poorer southern areas, but analysts said changes to prices of other commodities would be less controversial.

The cost to the treasury of direct handouts will be around 13 million dinars ($18 million) annually. Officials did not give costs for the current subsidies but said they were significantly higher than the direct handouts.

The ration system, which scales allotments according to family size, has been in place since the start of the 1990s to cushion the shock of a 1989 economic crisis when the dinar plummeted, sharply eroding the purchasing power of ordinary Jordanians.
Householders whose salaries fall under 500 dinars a month -- the same qualifying level as the old system -- will be offered 2.88 dinars per family member four times a year.

The move goes a considerable way to meet one element of Jordan's structural reforms under International Monetary Fund guidance, which involves phased lifting of price controls and food subsidies as part of liberalising its economy.
By cutting waste and directing aid to the neediest, the government hopes to end wide abuse of subsidies which cost it millions of dollars.
Last August Jordan began the first step towards dismantling the subsidies by raising bread prices. This followed a ballooning in the budget deficit because of a big bill for imported food.
But the bread price rise triggered the worst civil disorder in the impoverished south since 1989 riots.

Traders said the government's preparations for dismantling the ration system three months ahead of time aimed to help the private sector start to fill the vacuum after the state ended purchases for the ration cards.

The ration system accounted for a sizeable amount of total consumption of sugar and rice -- around 90,000 tonnes of sugar out of a total 150,000 tonnes of sugar annually and the bulk of the 90,000 tonnes of rice imported annually.
Dismantling the system will nearly end a two- decade monopoly of the state as importer for all grains, except wheat imports, for the time being.
A host of problems, not least financial, must be surmounted before the private sector can shoulder the burden of handling Jordan's annual 600,000 tonnes of wheat imports, traders said.
In a move expected to be followed by allowing private-sector imports of wheat, the government has sanctioned wheat imports for re-export to neighbouring states, traders said.

But traders have gradually been taking over as suppliers of sugar, rice, yellow corn and barley since the state last year began its first steps to dismantle its monopoly by allowing sale of these items to retailers.
The government's role will be restricted to overseeing price moves, quality control and maintaining storage silos it could lease to the private sector.
The government recently lifted price controls on a wide range of consumer items, including soft drinks and fresh produce, on which it had imposed maximum retail prices.
